Raytracing, where you're basically tracing/simulating photons from light source to camera, is an incredibly accurate way to render scenes. Photorealistic. However, it is very processing intensive and takes a long time. Algorithms were developed in the past that would let you basically just do a few simulations, end up with a noisy image with a bunch of missing data, and then kind of extrapolate the missing data into the end result. A little shortcut. But it doesn't work well with video. First, because you get a snowy kind of effect due to each frame being handled a little differently, and second, because each frame stands alone and doesn't provide information about the next frame. What they have managed to do is basically make it so that not individual frames are processed/generated, but the neural network is more aware of how to reconstruct the entire scene. No flickering. And it's even faster than before. It's neat.

In other words, as we can do when watching a low-quality video of some scene with the camera/object moving, where if you pause you see how grainy and indistinct each frame is. This is pretty cool. It sounds like the AI involves far less computation than doing the actual ray-tracing.
